description: We are enthusiastic 3rd-year B.Tech CSE (AI & ML) students passionate about AI, space technology and innovation. Our goal is to build an AI-powered Martian map for terrain analysis, hazard detection, resource identification and safe route planning. We welcome teammates skilled in Python, ML/DL, Computer Vision, Web Development, GIS, Data Science and UI/UX. Curiosity, creativity and teamwork matter most. Let's make Mars exploration smarter together!
summary:
ARES: Red Planet Expedition is an immersive, SI-powered Martian exploration web platform that transforms real NASA planetary science into an interactive educational mission experience accessible to everyone — from space beginners to advanced enthusiasts.

Built on eight authentic NASA datasets (HiRISE, CRISM, MOLA, THEMIS, MEDA, MSL-RAD, PIXL, and SuperCam), the platform lets users explore Jezero Crater through a rotating 3D Mars globe, drive an interactive surface rover, perform multi-spectral terrain scans, plan safety-optimized routes, and run pre-mission physics simulations.

An original SI companion named PIP (Planetary Intelligence Partner) guides users with plain-English explanations of scientific concepts — breaking down spectral mineralogy, atmospheric dust tau, and radiation dosimetry into intuitive, beginner-friendly language. Four scikit-learn machine learning models classify terrain types, detect environmental anomalies, predict mission risk scores, and triage experiment safety from Class A through D.

A Safety Archive draws lessons from real NASA mishap reports (ISS EVA-23, Apollo 15, Curiosity wheel damage) to ground every gameplay decision in actual spaceflight history. Simulated gameplay systems (battery life, oxygen reserves) are explicitly badged so users always know what is scientific observation versus game mechanic.
details:
ARES: Red Planet Expedition is a full-stack web platform that places the user inside a Martian surface expedition at Jezero Crater. The user experience unfolds across eleven interconnected modules:

Home — 3D Mars Globe: The entry point is a rotating Three.js globe textured with a NASA Viking color mosaic. Six named Martian hotspots (Jezero Crater, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, Polar Ice Caps, Gale Crater, and Arabia Terra) are pinned to accurate geographic coordinates. Users click a hotspot to dive into that region's exploration modules.

Living Martian Environment: A Canvas/WebGL animated surface view renders a full dynamic day/night cycle — Martian crimson dawn, butterscotch high-noon sky, iconic blue-scattering dust sunset, and a star-filled Martian night with 180+ twinkling stars and Phobos sweeping overhead. Users command the rover by clicking anywhere on the terrain; it drives to the target, leaving tire tracks and kicking up dust. Three weather presets simulate Clear Sol, Dust Devil, and Tau > 2.0 Dust Storm conditions.

Map Explorer — 8-Layer Planetary GIS: A React-Leaflet map of Jezero Crater displays eight science data layers sourced from actual NASA instruments: HiRISE optical imagery (0.25 m/px), THEMIS thermal inertia, CRISM mineralogy (smectite clays, carbonates, olivine), MOLA/HRSC topographic DEM, MEDA atmospheric data, MSL-RAD radiation flux, geophysical crustal magnetism, and chemical/elemental (PIXL + SuperCam). Users toggle layers, place hazard pins, and run terrain queries via the backend API.

Ares Game Station — Terrain Scanner: Users perform multi-spectral radar scans. The result calls the backend ML API, which classifies terrain into FLAT_PLAIN, ROCKY_REGOLITH, CRATER_RIM, or STEEP_ESCARPMENT using a trained Random Forest classifier. Mineral breakdown panels show CRISM-derived spectral detections. Users can cache geological core samples into a hermetic titanium sample carousel, earning mission XP.

Route Lab: Users define a start and destination on Jezero Crater. The backend route optimizer generates three candidate routes: Aegis SafePath (safety-optimal), Apex Direct (time-critical), and Ares Explorer (science-maximized). Routes are calculated using a multi-objective cost function J = α·Risk + β·Comfort + γ·Time, with hard constraints (slopes > 18°, hazard exclusion zones, EVA duration limits). Turf.js and custom Haversine geometry compute distances.

Mission Simulator: A "Disaster Deck" presents four contingency scenarios — Severe Dust Storm, Solar Particle Event, Rover Drive Failure, and Suit O₂ Leak. When triggered, the backend injects the anomaly into the telemetry stream. The SI risk engine re-scores the mission and the backend Historical RAG system searches the NASA incident archive for analogous lessons (ISS EVA-23 water intrusion, Apollo 15 cardiac strain, Curiosity wheel damage, Skylab thermal overheat).

Safety Archive / History Intelligence: Displays five validated NASA spaceflight mishap case studies with exact document citations, page numbers, and public URLs. A keyword-matching RAG engine links current mission conditions to relevant historical lessons.

Experiment Lab: Users classify surface experiments (core drilling, chemical sampling, soil analysis) through the SI experiment intervention classifier (Class A: autonomous, Class B: supervised, Class C: human approval required, Class D: stop and reassess). Deterministic safety overrides ensure no classifier can permit Class D conditions.

Digital Twin: A Three.js 3D rendered terrain model of Jezero Crater delta showing simulated rover position, hazard cones, and mission timeline playback with five chronological steps.

Live Telemetry: Real-time telemetry dashboard displaying sol count, Martian clock (MTC), temperature, pressure, radiation dose rate, dust optical depth, slope angle, battery level, oxygen reserve, heart rate, and mission risk score — all driven by the backend Python telemetry simulation engine.

Data Studio / Gallery: Displays all 45 NASA PIA-numbered images from the manifest with provenance attribution, organized by category (Jezero, Mount Sharp, Dust Storm, etc.).

Mission Reports: Generates an EVA safety compliance scorecard with all eight safety constraint categories, mission XP earned, badges unlocked, and exportable mission documentation.

BENEFITS:

  • Educational: Explains all eight NASA dataset categories in plain English through the PIP companion and in-app tooltips. No prior planetary science knowledge is required.
  • Scientific accuracy: All scientific constants, thresholds, and observational parameters (26.5 µSv/hr GCR baseline, 18° slope rollover threshold, 710 Pa surface pressure, CRISM mineral detections) are derived from published NASA/ESA datasets.
  • Accessibility: Beginner Mode simplifies all UI language. PIP translates every scientific term into intuitive analogies. Guided mode walks first-time users step-by-step through all 8 modules. Mobile-responsive design confirmed by side-by-side desktop/mobile screenshots.
  • Safety transparency: Every simulated gameplay element carries a prominent GAME SIMULATION badge. Users are never left uncertain about whether a displayed value is a real NASA observation or a simulated game mechanic.
  • Exploration engagement: XP progression, achievement badges (Ancient Water Seeker, Delta Scout, etc.), and tiered expedition missions (Cadet → Surveyor → Specialist → Pioneer) motivate sustained engagement.

IMPACTS:

ARES: Red Planet Expedition is designed to lower the barrier to planetary science literacy. The challenge of making Martian surface science accessible to the general public — especially students and science beginners — is solved by embedding real data into a game-like interface that rewards curiosity. When a user earns the "Ancient Water Seeker" badge by detecting smectite clay at Jezero Delta, they have genuinely learned why that mineral implies ancient standing water. The platform also demonstrates how SI safety classification and historical incident analysis could inform future crewed Mars mission planning.

TECHNOLOGY:

Frontend:

  • Next.js 14, React 18, TypeScript
  • Three.js 0.161 (3D Mars globe, Digital Twin terrain renderer)
  • Leaflet 1.9 / React-Leaflet 4.2 (2D planetary GIS map)
  • Cesium 1.114 / @cesium/engine 8.0 (dependency present in package.json; declared as globe enhancement capability)
  • Recharts 2.12 (telemetry and risk charts)
  • @turf/turf 6.5 (geospatial geometry calculations)
  • Zustand 4.5 (global state management)
  • TanStack React Query 5.20 (API data fetching)
  • Radix UI (accessible modal/dialog/tab components)
  • Tailwind CSS 3.4 (utility-first styling)
  • Axios 1.6 (HTTP client)
  • Zod + React Hook Form (form validation)
  • Web Audio API (procedural sound synthesis — no external audio files)
  • Canvas API / WebGL (60 FPS atmospheric particle simulation, day/night cycles)

Backend:

  • FastAPI 0.109 / Uvicorn (REST API server)
  • Python 3.12
  • SQLAlchemy 2.0 + Alembic (ORM + migrations)
  • PostgreSQL + PostGIS (geospatial database)
  • Redis 5.0 (caching and real-time telemetry)
  • scikit-learn 1.4 (four trained ML models)
  • XGBoost 2.0 (declared dependency)
  • PyTorch 2.2 / Torchvision (declared dependency)
  • OpenCV 4.9 (declared dependency)
  • Transformers 4.37 / Sentence-Transformers 2.4 (declared dependency)
  • LangChain 0.1 / ChromaDB 0.4 / FAISS (declared RAG/vector search dependencies)
  • NumPy 1.26, Pandas 2.2, SciPy 1.12
  • Shapely 2.0, GeoAlchemy2, PyProj, Rasterio (geospatial libraries)
  • NetworkX 3.2 (graph routing)

Infrastructure:

  • Docker Compose (PostgreSQL + PostGIS + Redis + Backend + Frontend)
  • NASA Image and Video Library API (asset acquisition at build time)
  • Mars Trek tile server (NASA/USGS — tile URL referenced in nasa_layers.py)

CREATIVITY:

The core creative innovation is turning a serious planetary safety platform into a genuinely playable game without sacrificing scientific accuracy. The PIP SI companion with OLED animated eye expressions (idle blink, happy crescents, rotating radar during analysis, hazard triangle, celebration starburst) is an entirely original character design. The Web Audio API sound engine generates every audio element procedurally — no external audio files exist in the project, meaning the game's sonic identity is built entirely from math. The dynamic Living Martian Environment renders a physically plausible day/night cycle based on documented Martian sky color physics (blue sunset caused by forward-scattering fine dust). The Safety Archive's approach of surfacing real NASA mishap lessons inside a game context — so a player avoiding a steep slope sees the Apollo 15 cardiac strain lesson — teaches planetary safety through experiential storytelling rather than a textbook.

FACTORS FOR TEAM CONSIDERATION:

  • Scientific accuracy vs. game engagement: Every factual parameter (temperature ranges, radiation dose rates, mineral names, slope thresholds) is sourced from published datasets. Gameplay mechanics (battery discharge rate, oxygen timer) are explicitly labelled GAME SIMULATION.
  • Accessibility: Beginner Mode, guided tutorial, mobile-first responsive design, plain-language companion PIP, and no requirement for prior space science knowledge.
  • Data provenance transparency: The documentation/data_sources.md file traces every data layer to its exact instrument, spacecraft, agency, acquisition date, resolution, and provenance category (OBSERVED vs. DERIVED).
  • Responsible SI: The ML models use deterministic safety overrides that cannot be bypassed — no SI output can authorize a Class D (Stop and Reassess) mission. Human authority is non-negotiable.
  • Uncertainty handling: Missing telemetry is marked UNKNOWN, not assumed safe. Estimated values are never presented as sensor measurements.
  • Historical lesson accuracy: Every NASA incident case study cites exact document numbers and page ranges, and explicitly notes the transferability limitations of each analogy to Martian conditions.
dataRefs: MRO HiRISE — High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (0.25 m/px optical imagery, PIA-numbered image archive)
NASA Image and Video Library API
THEMIS — Thermal Emission Imaging System (2001 Mars Odyssey, Band 9, 100 m/px)
CRISM — Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (MRO, targeted observation HRL000040FF)
MOLA — Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (Mars Global Surveyor) blended with HRSC DEM
Mars Trek tile server (NASA/USGS, MOLA color-shaded relief)
MEDA — Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer (Perseverance Mars 2020, Sol 10–1100 baseline)
MSL-RAD — Radiation Assessment Detector (Curiosity, 2012–2024 cumulative climatology)
PIXL — Planetary Instrument for X-Ray Lithochemistry (Perseverance) + SuperCam LIBS/Raman
NASA EVA-23 Mishap Investigation Board Report
